strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: predicting human response times under changing time-pressure cues. Combining task-derived neural features with an adjustable evidence-accumulation process is a plausible and potentially useful contribution.

The dataset contains 21,157 responses from 36 analyzed participants across four feedback conditions and two days. Random assignment, repeated measurements, and attention/anxiety ratings provide useful context for studying behavioral differences.

The experiments provide encouraging predictive evidence across four training strategies, including leave-one-participant-out evaluation. Figure 6 reports LOPO MAPE of 0.2905 for Hybrid DRL versus 0.3037 for Pure DRL, and the feature comparison supports the usefulness of the arithmetic agent’s representations.
The staged framework is understandable, and the manuscript provides data and code links, implementation details, and an explicit discussion of population and response-time modeling limitations.
weaknesses: The claimed connection to drift-diffusion modeling is insufficiently justified. Methods substitutes a sigmoid trajectory between an initial value and an SVC-derived probability threshold, without specifying a diffusion process or deriving why classification probabilities represent evidence boundaries. This may be a useful heuristic accumulator, but established DDM interpretations do not automatically apply. The cognitive justification requires validation beyond response-time prediction.

The central interpretability claim exceeds the evidence. Training supervises terminal response time, which generally cannot identify the intermediate sequence of evidence adjustments. Figure 7 also shows substantial inferred 'time-pressure effects' in the no-pressure condition, suggesting that these trajectories can absorb baseline prediction errors. Agreement with group-level response-time trends is therefore insufficient to establish the proposed psychological mechanism. Independent process measurements, controlled cue-timing interventions, or explicit identifiability analyses would strengthen this claim.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of the proposed hybrid design. Pure DRL uses concatenated Inception-V3 video features, whereas Hybrid DRL uses a different frame-level encoder; action scaling and episode structure also differ substantially. These differences confound both accuracy and training-time comparisons. Matched architectures, supervised predictors conditioned on pressure and elapsed time, conventional accumulation models, and ablations removing frame information are needed to establish the value of this particular combination relative to existing approaches.

The predictive improvements lack uncertainty estimates. For example, general-level MAPE changes from 0.3034 to 0.2999, a small difference whose reliability cannot be assessed from the reported plots. Repeated training runs and participant-level paired uncertainty estimates are needed. The reported 4.42-versus-38.30-minute convergence comparison also lacks a sufficiently explicit, comparable convergence criterion.

The evaluation protocol is ambiguous across pipeline stages. The manuscript does not clearly identify which trials train the supposedly pressure-free SVC/SVR baseline or whether these models are refitted within every outer split, particularly LOPO. Consequently, exclusion of held-out human responses cannot be verified. Random trial splits and chronological plotting of LOPO predictions also do not establish forecasting performance on future sessions or generalization to unseen feedback schedules.

The behavioral findings require more careful statistical reporting. Only 7–10 participants remain per condition, the criterion for excluding three 'extreme outliers' is unspecified, and the handling of the ten-second response-time limit is unclear. The stated use of paired post hoc tests between independently assigned groups needs clarification or correction. These details matter because the reported response-time group effect is modest and supports subsequent interpretation of the learned trajectories.

Important reproduction details remain absent from the manuscript, including the exact sigmoid parameterization and evidence-update equation, the value of the action-scaling factor lambda, and numerical thresholds for the adaptive feedback rule. These omissions concern the central mechanism and experimental conditions, rather than minor presentation corrections.
